sheets.heading: Year Key Event / Milestone
sheets.text:
Year Key Event / Milestone

1949 RBI Nationalised (January 1) via the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948;

Banking Regulation Act, 1949 enacted.

1955 SBI established (July 1) by taking over the Imperial Bank of India under the State Bank

of India Act, 1955.

1956 LIC nationalised (September 1) through the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956,

merging over 240 private insurers and societies.

1959 SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act passed, bringing 8 princely state-associated banks under

SBI ownership (later known as SBI Associate Banks).

1969 14 major commercial banks nationalised (July 19) having deposits $\\ge$ ₹50 crore under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969.

1975 Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) established (October 2) following the Narasimham

Working Group recommendations (Prathama Bank was the first).

1980

6 more commercial banks nationalised (April 15) having deposits $\\ge$ ₹200 crore (Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab & Sind Bank, Vijaya Bank).

1982 NABARD established (July 12) under the B. Sivaraman Committee recommendations

via the NABARD Act, 1981; EXIM Bank set up.

1990 SIDBI established (April 2) as the principal financial institution for promotion and

financing of MSMEs.

1991 Narasimham Committee I report submitted, kicking off economic liberalisation, entry

of private banks, and deregulation of interest rates.

1993 First major PSB merger: New Bank of India merged into Punjab National due to financial distress, reducing nationalised banks from 20 to 19.

Bank (PNB)

2017 Mega SBI Consolidation: 5 associate banks (SBBJ, SBH, SBM, SBP, SBT) and Bharatiya

Mahila Bank (BMB) merged into the State Bank of India.

2019 Bank of Baroda Consolidation (April 1): Dena Bank and Vijaya Bank merged into Bank

of Baroda.

Year Key Event / Milestone

2020

Mega PSB Consolidation (April 1):

10 Public Sector Banks merged into 4 anchors:

1\) Oriental Bank of Commerce + United Bank of India --\> Punjab National

Bank 2) Syndicate Bank --\> Canara Bank 3) Andhra Bank + Corporation Bank --\> Union Bank of India 4) Allahabad Bank --\> Indian Bank

(Reduced the number of Public Sector Banks in India to 12)

2021+

Strategic Disinvestment & Modernisation Policy: The Central Government approved a policy framework for the potential privatisation/stake reduction of selected public sector lenders, retaining a minimum presence in strategic sectors while prioritizing digital banking units (DBUs) and PSB governance reforms.

sheets.heading: Liberalisation Globalisation Remove/reduce domestic controls Integrate with world economy De-licensing International tra
sheets.text:
Liberalisation Globalisation Remove/reduce domestic controls Integrate with world economy De-licensing International trade Deregulation Foreign investment Reduce restrictions Technology flows Import liberalisation MNC participation Greater market orientation Greater global integration

Keyword Mechanism Note

1991 NEP Strategy

Introduced to address the severe 1991 Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis.

Reform Classification

LPG model: Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation.

Stabilisation: Short-term, demand- side, addresses inflation and macroeconomic imbalances.

Structural Adjustment: Long-term, supply-side, addresses industrial, trade, financial, and investment structures.

Stabilisation is strictly short-term, while Structural Adjustment is long- term.

Liberalisation Focus

Removal of state controls via industrial de-licensing, import deregulation, and private sector expansion.

New Industrial Policy announced on 24 July 1991 was the primary starting anchor.

Liberalisation Instruments

Lowers cost of technology and capital equipment, boosting domestic manufacturing competitiveness.

Globalisation Definition

Reduction of import duties on capital goods.

Integration of the domestic economy with the world economy

Facilitated expanded entry and participation of Multinational

Keyword Mechanism Note

via trade, capital (FDI), and cross-

Corporations (MNCs). border technology.

Post-1991 Key Trends

Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows increased, foreign exchange reserves expanded, and India's share in global exports grew.

Trap: "Share of agriculture in GDP increased enormously after 1991 reforms" is FALSE (agriculture's share declined).

Industrial Chronology

1951: IDR Act (Licensing framework established)

1956: Industrial Policy Resolution (Public and joint sector dominance)

1991: New Industrial Policy (Massive de-licensing and deregulation)

SEZ Policy Link Announced on 1 April 2000 under

the Globalisation framework.

Primary objectives: boost export competitiveness, attract FDI, and create an internationally competitive trade environment.

sheets.heading: Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) Cash Reserve ratio (CRR) Liquid assets maintained by bank itself Cash reserve maintained
sheets.text:
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) Cash Reserve ratio (CRR) Liquid assets maintained by bank itself Cash reserve maintained with RBI Cash + Gold + Securities Cash Bank's own holdings RBI-held reserve Used to regulate credit/liquidity Used to regulate credit/liquidity Government securities commonly used No interest on CRR reserves

Keyword Mechanism Note

Minimum percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) SLR Definition

that commercial banks must maintain in liquid assets before lending.

SLR is maintained by the bank with itself, NOT deposited with the RBI (unlike CRR, which goes to RBI).

Eligible SLR Assets

Most commonly held in Government Securities (G-Secs) because they earn interest income while meeting statutory requirements.

SLR Increase (Tight Stance)

Liquid cash, gold, and other unencumbered approved securities.

Bank locks higher percentage of funds in liquid assets, reducing investible loan funds.

Credit creation decreases, money supply contracts, and inflationary pressures are controlled.

SLR Decrease (Expansionary Stance)

Bank holds fewer funds in mandatory liquid assets, freeing up capital for loans.

Lending capacity expands, credit creation increases, and broader economic activity is stimulated.

Counter- Inflationary Use

Raising the SLR acts as a direct contractionary quantitative credit control tool.

Used by the central bank during inflation to rein in excessive commercial bank credit growth.
